This scroll recounts the goddess’s origin, miracles, protection of women and children, and pilgrimage ethos of Taishan. Catalogued among North China sectarian and popular religious performance texts; it documents how a major Daoist mountain goddess was popularized through vernacular scripture.
entries.key_passages: 泰山娘娘显灵应，庇佑众生保安康 (typical baojuan refrain pattern)
entries.application: Relevant to BaZi via the Taishan destiny complex (life–death registration, offspring, and ‘maternal’ protective spirits); for cultivation, models devotion, vow-keeping, and feminine divine power.
entries.related: 历代神仙通鉴; 香山寶卷; 何仙姑寶卷

entries.deep_essence: One of the most famous Chinese baojuan, narrating the legend of Princess Miaoshan (妙善), who refuses marriage, endures persecution, and becomes Guanyin of Xiangshan (Fragrant Mountain). Ming–Qing printed and manuscript versions were performed widely; scholarship (e.g., studies of baojuan and Guanyin cults) treats it as a primary vehicle for female renunciation ideals, filiality paradox, and the popularization of Guanyin’s Chinese biography. Structure: prose narrative + sung verses + moral exhortation.
entries.key_passages: 妙善公主出家修行，香山成道，观音救苦
entries.application: Though Buddhist-flavored, it deeply shaped Chinese religious subjectivity of renunciation and compassionate response—parallel to Daoist renunciation paths; in fate discourse, Guanyin’s rescue is often invoked against hard BaZi configurations.
entries.related: 劉香女寶卷; 目连救母出离地狱生天宝卷; 何仙姑寶卷

entries.deep_essence: A precious scroll dedicated to He Xiangu, the sole female member of the Eight Immortals. It recounts her miraculous birth or vocation, dietary/sexual renunciation, attainment of immortality, and salvific interventions—especially for women. As with other immortal baojuan, performance settings included temple fairs and women’s religious gatherings. Scholarship places it in the broader Eight Immortals popular literature that bridges elite neidan symbolism and folk narrative.
entries.key_passages: 何仙姑持荷修真，得道飞升，普度善信
entries.application: Directly relevant to female cultivation models and to the Eight Immortals as archetypes in popular fate culture; He Xiangu often symbolizes purity, longevity practices, and yin-path attainment.
entries.related: 香山寶卷; 劉香女寶卷; 历代神仙通鉴

entries.deep_essence: The Baojuan of Liu Xiangnü (劉香女), a classic Ming precious scroll about a devout laywoman who endures family opposition, practices pure vegetarian Buddhist-Daoist hybrid piety, and achieves salvation while converting household members. Extensively studied in baojuan scholarship as a window into women’s domestic religion, gender, and sectarian ethics in late imperial China. Narrative stress falls on patience under suffering, sutra recitation, and the domestic altar as a field of cultivation.
entries.key_passages: 刘香女苦修持斋，感化家人，终得善果
entries.application: Models lay cultivation under constrained social destiny (family pressure, gender roles)—a narrative analogue to ‘working with’ a difficult BaZi rather than fleeing the world; emphasizes merit, speech-karma, and household harmony.
entries.related: 香山寶卷; 何仙姑寶卷; 叹世无为卷

entries.deep_essence: The ‘original biography’ of Qingshui Zushi (清水祖師, Patriarch of Clear Water), the Song-dynasty Fujian monk-thaumaturge Chen Puzu (陳普足) of Anxi, later deified across Minnan, Taiwan, and Southeast Asia. The benzhuan genre fixes miracle cycles: rain-making, healing, mountain austerities at Qingshui Rock, and posthumous spirit manifestations. Used by temples as authoritative origin narrative alongside liturgical and pilgrimage practice; exists in temple prints and local gazetteer-linked versions.
entries.key_passages: 陈普足栖隐清水岩，祷雨济民，坐化显圣
entries.application: Cultivation relevance: mountain asceticism, rain-and-drought response, and protective patronage; in BaZi/popular fate culture, Qingshui Zushi is petitioned for crisis resolution and community protection, showing how local immortals mediate destiny.
entries.related: 安溪清水岩志; 龍湖集; 历代神仙通鉴

entries.deep_essence: A temple/mountain gazetteer (山志/岩志) for Qingshui Rock in Anxi, Fujian—the cult center of Qingshui Zushi. Typical contents: topography, founding legends, reconstruction dates, miracle records, stele inscriptions, pilgrimage routes, and lists of donors and abbots. As a local religious-historical source, it anchors the hagiography of the Patriarch in place-based institutional memory and is cited in studies of Minnan temple networks and overseas Chinese cult transmission.
entries.key_passages: 清水岩峰峦秀异，祖师道场，灵异昭著 (gazetteer-style framing)
entries.application: Documents how sacred geography supports cultivation and vow culture; for BaZi practice communities, local zhi texts explain why certain temple gods ‘respond’ in specific regions and lineage networks.
entries.related: 清水祖師本傳; 龍湖集; 靈應泰山娘娘寶卷

entries.deep_essence: Longhu ji (龍湖集) is associated with literary and religious writings linked to Longhu (Dragon Lake) sites or lineages—most prominently the Zhang Heavenly Masters’ Longhu Shan cultural sphere, or local Longhu literary collections depending on edition. In Daoist bibliographic contexts, Longhu-related collectanea preserve poetry, ritual prefaces, and Heavenly Master institution materials. Catalog entries and reprints should be checked against specific editions (literary vs. Daoist), as multiple works share or approximate this title; scholarly discussion of Longhu literature centers on Zhengyi authority, talismanic tradition, and mountain-as-axis symbolism.
entries.key_passages: 龙虎山为道教正一祖庭，符箓宗坛 (institutional essence reflected in Longhu literature)
entries.application: Zhengyi talismanic and ordination frameworks that still structure how many BaZi/fate masters understand celestial offices, seals, and legitimate ritual intervention in destiny.
entries.related: 金箓分灯捲帘科仪全集; 清水祖師本傳; 撼龍經

entries.deep_essence: The Hanlong jing (‘Classic of Shaking the Dragon’), a foundational form-school (形勢) fengshui text traditionally attributed to Yang Yunsong (楊筠松) of the Tang. It teaches how to ‘shake’ or awaken the dragon vein: reading mountain ridges, water mouths, xue (穴) sites, and the motion of qi through landscape morphology. Circulated widely in geomantic corpora; modern critical study treats it as core of Jiangxi form school theory, often paired with Yilong jing and related Yang-gong texts. Dense technical verse with later commentaries.
entries.key_passages: 寻龙分枝拨脉，点穴乘气；龙昂气壮，穴的则灵
entries.application: Directly adjacent to BaZi: form fengshui and destiny analysis were historically co-practiced; dragon-vein theory supplies the spatial half of ‘time (BaZi) + space (kanyu)’ fate craft and of choosing cultivation retreats.
entries.related: 龍湖集; 历代神仙通鉴; 金箓分灯捲帘科仪全集

entries.deep_essence: One of the Five Books in Six Volumes (五部六冊) of Luo Qing (羅清), founder of the Luo Teaching (羅教/无为教) in the late Ming. Tanshi wuwei juan (‘Scroll of Sighing at the World and Non-Action’) critiques worldly attachment, clerical formalism, and false practice, urging return to the unborn vacuum (真空家乡) and wuwei realization. Extensively studied in scholarship on Ming sectarian religion (e.g., works on Luo jiao and baojuan). Banned at times as ‘heterodox’ yet hugely influential on later precious-scroll theology.
entries.key_passages: 叹世无常，无为得真；归家认祖，脱离苦海
entries.application: Offers a radical ‘destiny exit’ via recognition of original nature rather than ritual accumulation; useful contrast to liturgical jilian texts—cultivation as insight into emptiness of saṃsāric BaZi-bound existence.
entries.related: 苦功悟道卷; 破邪显证钥匙卷; 销释真空宝卷

entries.deep_essence: Another of Luo Qing’s Five Books in Six Volumes: ‘Scroll of Awakening to the Way through Bitter Effort.’ It autobiographically and didactically recounts the intensity of seeking—years of austerity, doubt, and breakthrough into the teaching of the unborn. Scholars read it as the experiential backbone of Luo jiao: enlightenment framed as hard practice culminating in sudden clarity of zhenkong (true emptiness). Style mixes vernacular sermon and scriptural quotation.
entries.key_passages: 苦功参究，忽然顿悟；真空家乡，无生父母
entries.application: Models the ‘bitter effort’ phase of cultivation before insight—comparable to refining a difficult chart through discipline; the unborn-parent metaphor refigures fate as return to pre-natal origin (a bridge to Daoist xiantian discourse).
entries.related: 叹世无为卷; 破邪显证钥匙卷; 销释真空宝卷

entries.deep_essence: Luo Qing’s ‘Key Scroll for Destroying Heresy and Manifesting Proof,’ part of the Five Books in Six Volumes. It polemically refutes rival teachings and ‘false masters,’ presenting Luo’s doctrine as the master-key (钥匙) that unlocks true salvation. Important for historians of Chinese new religious movements: it shows how sectarian identity was built by scriptural critique and by claiming a single decisive dharma-gate. Language is vernacular, combative, and full of metaphor of locks, keys, and clear proof.
entries.key_passages: 破邪显正，钥匙一把；开通心地，立见真宗
entries.application: Relevant as a cautionary and comparative text: how fate/cultivation markets produce orthodoxy claims; also encodes a soteriology in which correct view, not only calendar technique, determines liberation.
entries.related: 叹世无为卷; 苦功悟道卷; 销释真空宝卷

entries.deep_essence: A precious scroll of the ‘explicating true emptiness’ (銷釋真空) family, circulating in Ming–Qing sectarian and popular Buddhist-Daoist milieus. It expounds zhenkong thought—often aligned with Luo-ist or related Huangtian/Hongyang networks—through sung narrative and didactic verse: the world is illusory, the home-village of true emptiness is the goal, and ritual formalism without inner awakening is insufficient. Multiple related titles exist; cataloguers group them among non-canonical baojuan preserved in library and field collections.
entries.key_passages: 销释真空，归家认祖；不生不灭，本来面目
entries.application: Supplies the metaphysical ‘pre-Heaven’ emptiness frame that some modern BaZi/xuanxue readers pair with chart analysis: techniques handle houtian patterns; vacuum teaching aims at what precedes patterned fate.
entries.related: 叹世无为卷; 苦功悟道卷; 破邪显证钥匙卷

entries.name_han: 目连救母出离地狱生天宝卷
entries.deep_essence: A major baojuan retelling of the Mulian (Maudgalyāyana) saving-his-mother cycle: Mulian’s mother falls into hell for karmic sins; Mulian’s quest, aided by Buddha’s instruction and the Ullambana rite, frees her to rebirth in heaven. Chinese versions fuse Buddhist jātaka material with local opera and ritual performance; performed especially at Ghost Festival. Scholarship treats it as central to Chinese ideas of filial salvation, purgatory bureaucracy, and merit transfer—deeply interwoven with Daoist jilian/shishi practice in the same festival complex.
entries.key_passages: 目连救母出地狱，承佛慈力得生天
entries.application: Core narrative for ancestral karma and intergenerational destiny—the ethical backdrop to why BaZi/cultivation cultures stress filial rites, Zhongyuan feeding of ghosts, and rewriting family karmic debt.
entries.related: 青玄集要炼度施食科仪; 全真青玄济炼铁罐施食全集; 香山寶卷

entries.deep_essence: A precious scroll on the Fifth Chan Patriarch Hongren of Huangmei (黃梅五祖). It popularizes Chan patriarchal legend—Hongren’s life, the transmission contest, and the Sixth Patriarch Huineng’s emergence—in baojuan performance style for lay audiences. Functions as vernacular Chan hagiography rather than monastic yulu; reinforces East Mountain teaching’s place in popular religious memory and the drama of sudden enlightenment transmission.
entries.key_passages: 黄梅五祖传衣法，能者得之悟无生
entries.application: Transmission and ‘mind-seal’ themes parallel Daoist lineage investiture; for cultivation under BaZi constraints, it models that awakening can cut across hereditary and social destiny when the right dharma-affinity appears.
entries.related: 销释真空宝卷; 苦功悟道卷; 香山寶卷

entries.deep_essence: A precious scroll devoted to the Tudigong (土地公), the local earth god of Chinese popular religion. Narrative and hymn sections praise his protection of fields, households, and community boundaries, recount origin or miracle tales, and teach moral reciprocity with offerings. Though low in the pantheon, Tudi is ubiquitous in temple and domestic cult; the baojuan form elevates him into performative scripture. Field and library catalogues of baojuan routinely list Tudi-related scrolls among village performance repertoires.
entries.key_passages: 土地神祇守一方，善恶分明佑善良
entries.application: In BaZi/fengshui practice, the earth god is the immediate spirit of site and soil—mediating dragon-vein ethics, household luck, and local ‘response’; cultivation here means right relation to place, not only abstract star qi.
entries.related: 撼龍經; 靈應泰山娘娘寶卷; 历代神仙通鉴
